title: Scalable photonic reservoir computing for parallel machine learning tasks

paper_content.abstract: Neuromorphic photonics enables brain-inspired information processing with higher bandwidth and lower energy consumption than traditional electronics, addressing the growing computational demands of the Internet of Things, cloud services, and edge computing. However, even current state-of-the-art electronic and photonic platforms are incapable of delivering the scalable throughput, multitasking processing, and energy efficiency required by these applications. Here, we demonstrate a tunable photonic reservoir computing device based on a nonlinear amplifying loop mirror (NALM), leveraging a time-delayed, single-unit, all-optical architecture. By combining dense temporal encoding with wavelength-division multiplexing, the system supports concurrent multitasking across independent data channels, enabling scalable computational performance without additional hardware complexity. Experiments and theoretical validation on classification and prediction benchmarks demonstrate the device’s performance, achieving a throughput of 20 tera-operations-per-second and an energy efficiency of 4.4 fJ per operation. These results highlight a promising path towards reconfigurable, compact, and high-performance photonic processors for real-time intelligent applications.
paper_content.introduction:
The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) has revolutionized data processing, driving demand for computational platforms that are capable of handling vast amounts of data with high processing speed and minimal latency1,2. Neuromorphic photonics presents a promising solution to these challenges2–8 as it leverages optical systems to emulate neural networks, thus providing higher bandwidth, faster speeds, lower energy consumption, and smaller footprints compared to traditional electronic processors7,9–11. This solution can also lower carbon emissions, especially when training on large datasets. However, existing photonic architectures have critical limitations in computational throughput, energy efficiency, and latency, thus hindering their ability to meet the growing computational needs of AI, deep learning12, and other real-time-based applications13,14. Neuromorphic computing frameworks, such as extreme learning machines15, wave-based neural networks16, and reservoir computing (RC)17,18, have emerged as compelling approaches for the efficient implementation of photonic processing devices for ML.

Optical RC systems exploit physical dynamics to process input data, thus reducing training time and complexity while improving computational efficiency. To date, single-node optical RC architectures have been demonstrated using active components (such as semiconductor lasers19, amplifiers20,21, and electro-optic modulators22,23), as well as passive components24 (including saturable absorbers25,26 and photodiodes27). Despite significant progress, current RC implementations remain limited by their inherent architecture, in which nodes are created and interconnected through feedback mechanisms27,28. These mechanisms simplify the design by generating virtual nodes, but also introduce latency and limit processing speed, which is defined as system throughput (i.e., the total number of operations per second across all input data streams within a single reservoir unit). Recent efforts to increase computational throughput in RC have focused on faster electro-optical modulation and advanced data encoding schemes, such as pulse-amplitude modulation29–31 (PAM), often paired with wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM). However, these methods frequently rely on sequential sweeping across WDM channels32–34, or time-interleaving techniques35–39, which both introduce throughput latency and prevent the concurrent execution of independent tasks. Additional attempts at further scaling up performance have involved adding components or increasing the number and dimensionality of computational layers and readout components5,39. Typically, these result in decreased energy efficiency and processing speeds. Furthermore, existing WDM-based RC architectures21,38,39 also have limited tunability, when design constraints inherently fix both the reservoir memory and the activation function. At the same time, nonlinearity is introduced electronically at the input/output stage, resulting in optical-to-electrical-to-optical (OEO) latency and thus limiting the richness of reservoir dynamics. Such constraints significantly reduce system flexibility and adaptability for diverse ML tasks. Additionally, architectures employing spectral mixing approaches21 encounter nonlinear crosstalk40, which, in turn, limits the number of independently encoded channels and consequently degrades system accuracy and scalability.

To address these challenges, we demonstrate an RC device based on a nonlinear amplifying loop mirror (NALM) architecture. We leverage the NALM configuration for its proven ability to generate highly stable and nonlinear dynamics41–44, which are essential for optical reservoir computing. These dynamics enhance the reservoir’s computational capacity by enabling complex input mapping into a high-dimensional state space, thereby improving sensitivity to extremely small signal variations45,46. The intrinsic stability of the NALM ensures consistent classification performance, even under noisy or fluctuating input conditions.

Our device features an integrated nonlinear spiral waveguide (SW) and a semiconductor optical amplifier (SOA), both of which modulate the NALM overall nonlinear transfer function (i.e., the reservoir activation function). In contrast to previous RC implementations that rely on SOAs operating in saturation, whether in unidirectional configurations47–49 or through cross-gain modulation50,51, we set the SOA below saturation for all our experiments. Saturated SOAs exhibit plateaued gain, limiting the dynamic range and tunability of the nonlinear response. The unsaturated regime, on the other hand, allows for precise tunability of the gain and, therefore, of the reservoir activation function. Furthermore, by adjusting the intensity of the propagating field using a variable optical attenuator (VOA), we achieve additional control over the reservoir’s fading memory response, significantly enhancing both versatility and stability for diverse computational tasks.

In line with the standard single-node reservoir computing framework, we establish virtual nodes within the reservoir via time-multiplexing, with training restricted to the readout layer. However, by employing multiple synchronized continuous-wave (CW) laser sources, our device can support multi-task processing across wavelength channels. This enables true concurrency for parallel data injection, both for the same or different machine learning tasks. The latter significantly reduces hardware complexity and addresses scalability and performance bottlenecks in earlier architectures. As a result, we have achieved a throughput of up to 20 tera-operations per second (TOPS), consuming only a few femtojoules per operation, while maintaining high accuracy in both classification and regression tasks. The device setup, as depicted in Fig. 1, encompasses a figure-eight fiber cavity that enables efficient multi-processing and provides rich system tunability. Such figure-eight fiber shapes can produce a range of coherent nonlinear dynamics, both with41 and without42,43 CW injection. By leveraging dynamic regimes and higher dimensionality enabled by virtual nodes, we accurately separate and classify continuous-valued input signals, even when they are complex and highly nonlinear.
paper_content.results:
We benchmarked our device to solve linearly inseparable problems using the m-bit delayed parity task, also known as the generalized exclusive OR (XOR)16. This nonlinear task performs the XOR operation between the current bit and the m prior bits stored in the reservoir memory and classifies the resulting sequences into two distinct classes. We injected a pseudorandom binary sequence (PRBS) of 4000 bits into a single-wavelength channel using a CW source (see the setup in Fig. 1) in the input device loop. Through the encoding procedure described in the Methods section entitled “Device architecture”, we generated 161 virtual processing nodes. Consistent with the RC paradigm, training was applied exclusively to the output weights, while the internal node connection weights remained fixed. These internal weights are inherently defined by the device configuration and the specific components that were employed, such as the SOA, the integrated SW, and the variable optical attenuator (VOA) (see Supplementary Note 1). We applied ridge regression27 to determine the optimal output weights required to reconstruct the target signal. The accuracy of the trained model was evaluated using standard performance metrics, such as the normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE).

We investigated the classification performance when varying the SOA gain and the signal attenuation of the VOA by tuning their driving voltages, VSOA and VVOA, respectively (which correspond to a specific level of amplification gain g and attenuation level AVOA). Figure 2 shows the NRMSE maps (g and AVOA) for 2-bit, 3-bit, and 4-bit delayed sequences in (a), (b), and (c), respectively. For the 2-bit XOR, we achieved 100% classification accuracy for the validation dataset, as shown in the dark-blue shaded region of Fig. 2a, which is defined by g < 8.3 dB and AVOA < 4.9 dB (VSOA < 0.8 V and VVOA > 3 V). These values delimit operational regimes characterized by reduced nonlinear contributions from the SOA and by short fading memory controlled by the VOA.

For the 3- and 4-bit XOR sequences, a further nonlinear contribution to the overall response (i.e., the activation function) of the reservoir is required to enhance the output separability and reduce the NRMSE16. This is achieved when setting g > 6.1 dB and AVOA > 0.3 dB (VSOA > 0.5 V and VVOA > 1.5 V), respectively, for the 3- and 4-bit cases. This enables the device to achieve accuracies of 97% and 80% (with NRMSEs of 3% and 20%), as reported in Fig. 2b and c.

Reservoir tunability enables handling ML tasks with varying degrees of data separability and temporal correlations, as evident in the analysis of the effect on the propagating input signals as a function of the two tunable parameters. When an input signal, such as an optical field, enters the device reservoir loop through the 3 dB (50:50) input beamsplitter (Fig. 1), it separates into propagating and counter-propagating field components. Their phase difference, after they propagate in opposite directions and recombine at the beamsplitter, is affected by sequences of amplification and nonlinear interactions mediated by the intensity-dependent Kerr nonlinearity in the integrated SW52,53. During such an interaction, an increase in the amplification gain causes the SOA to contribute additional nonlinear responses, thereby enhancing classification performance when further nonlinear contributions are required54, without altering the physical reservoir topology. This unsaturated operational regime enables us to implement a controllable mechanism mediated by tunable parameters, allowing for the exploitation of nonlinearities arising from controlled optical feedback and intensity-dependent interference within the NALM. This approach allows for precise and reconfigurable reservoir functionality. In contrast to the cross-gain saturation-based nonlinearities demonstrated in earlier works50,51. Our architecture provides greater flexibility and control over reservoir dynamics.

Generally, in time-delayed RC, a higher reservoir nonlinearity can impair the fading memory, which is determined by the system’s round-trip time46,55. By fine-tuning the input intensity attenuation through VVOA, we can modify the strength of the interconnection among the reservoir virtual nodes. This adjustment regulates the amount of circulating intra-cavity power per round-trip, thereby compensating for the reservoir’s diminished capacity to store bits within its fading memory56.

Multi-processing and parallel operation
We established the multi-processing capabilities of our device by carrying out two well-known ML benchmarks in parallel: the Mackey-Glass (MG) and the 10th-order Nonlinear Auto Regressive Moving Average (NARMA10) time series prediction tasks. These two tasks address the nonlinearity and memory of the reservoir, challenging the trade-off that occurs between them. The chaotic nature of the MG system, with high sensitivity to initial conditions, requires a reservoir with high nonlinearity. On the other hand, NARMA10 requires a reservoir with a long fading memory to efficiently retain temporal dependencies among data points across various round-trips. Therefore, by performing both tasks simultaneously, we demonstrate the universal multi-processing potential of our device in tackling both of these diverse ML tasks.

We use two wavelength channels, one at 1549.2 nm for the MG task and the second at 1549.4 nm for NARMA10. Crosstalk effects were reduced by applying a 0.2 nm spectral separation between the channels. We generated 1200 data points for each time series and encoded them onto Nv = 161 virtual nodes in the reservoir through dense WDM. Based on the results of the m-bit XOR task (where the highest accuracies are achieved within the dark-blue-shaded regions shown in Fig. 2a), we found that the best performance can be reached with g = 10.3 dB (VSOA = 1.5 V) and AVOA ≈ 0 dB (VVOA = 0.5 V). We applied offline training and cross-validation57 independently on the two de-multiplexed outputs to obtain the weights that minimize the NRMSE between the targeted and predicted outputs. The results in Fig. 3 show misclassification rates of just 6% for MG and 1% for NARMA10, indicating high classification accuracy in both cases.

Computational scalability of the device
We demonstrate system scalability through both increased bit density and parallel channel encoding, enabling the scaling up of computational throughput without requiring additional physical nodes. We next applied the device to solve a real-world task: recovering a nonlinearly perturbed telecom signal. Signal distortion, attenuation, dispersion, noise, and crosstalk originating from fiber propagation can all degrade or disrupt communications. Therefore, channel recovery techniques are essential for preserving signal integrity, minimizing downtime, and ensuring quality of service in networks29,58. This requires nonlinear, low-latency, high-speed processing capabilities. As shown by previous benchmarks, our device offers features that can meet these requirements, and its computational speed can be further enhanced by employing a dense information encoding scheme alongside multi-channel processing. The dense encoding scheme (see the Methods section entitled “Information encoding and readout”) enables us to inject multiple bits per wavelength channel into the reservoir, thereby increasing speed without adding extra computational units.

We generated a PRBS of 5×(215 − 1) bits and electro-optically encoded it onto a CW carrier signal. We then let the signal propagate through 60 km of standard single-mode fiber (SMF). Here, the once pristine signal experiences dispersion and nonlinear distortion, including cross-phase modulation and four-wave mixing, both of which are influenced by fiber length and signal intensity. Figure 4a and b show the time traces of the modulated field intensity using PAM30,31 before and after propagation, respectively, along with their corresponding eye diagrams. The distorted signal is then distributed and encoded across five independent channels, spaced at 0.2 nm intervals around 1550 nm (as shown in Fig. 4b), which we process concurrently via dense WDM. The number of encoding channels is limited only by the available CW sources and electro-optical intensity modulators (IMs). The representative bit sequences before and after recovery are shown in the Supplementary Fig. 5.

We trained and validated the output weights for each channel across four virtual nodes using the encoding technique and offline ridge regression. The bit error rate (BER, the metric that quantifies the percentage of misclassified bits in the recovered sequence) is shown in Fig. 5(a), illustrating the individual channels and different input power levels (Pin = 2.6 dBm, 3.8 dBm, 4.2 dBm, 4.6 dBm, 5.0 dBm, and 5.4 dBm), which are commonly used in telecommunications. We observed that the BER decreases as the input signal power increases, due to improved signal-to-noise ratio.

This change occurs regardless of the surge in distortion due to the intensity-dependent Kerr effect on transmission, which our approach can compensate for. The lowest BER value is 2×10−4 at 5.4 dBm of input power, representing a 145-fold improvement compared to the preprocessed distorted signal (see Fig. 5b). The inset of Fig. 5c displays a segment of the original bit sequence alongside the corresponding distorted optical signal, measured after propagation through the 60 km fiber link (prior to recovery processing). Figure 5d shows the recovered bit sequence at an input power of 5.4 dBm, with a zoomed-in segment highlighting the bit errors (marked with red squares).

The experimental results were validated using the model derived from the generalized nonlinear Schrodinger equation59 (GNLSE) (see Supplementary Note 1). We report the average BER over the five wavelength channels (red line) and the simulated BER values (black dots) in Fig. 5a. We observed excellent agreement between the numerical predictions and our experimental results, confirming the accuracy of our model.

We can quantify the throughput of our device in terms of MAC (multiply-and-accumulate) operations per second for parallel signal recovery. The device achieves a 2.7 Tera-MACs-1. From the MAC calculation, we estimate a speed of 20 Tera-operations per second (TOPS) for our device. In terms of energy efficiency, the overall power consumption of the processing unit is approximately 87 mW, leading to consumption of ~4.4 fJ OP-1 (see Supplementary Note 4 for detailed calculations), which outperforms both state-of-the-art fiber-based optical neural networks and photonic chips5,8,35,60–62. See Table 1 for a numerical comparison.
paper_content.methods:
Device architecture
The device’s figure-eight cavity design (see Fig. 1) can be divided into input, processing (i.e., the reservoir or unit), and output stages, all of which contribute to the overall round-trip time and thereby cause the reservoir’s memory to fade. The input loop comprises a variable optical VOA (Thorlabs, V1550A) that controls the signal power, a 10:90 coupler that monitors the system, a 50:50 coupler that injects the modulated signal, and a second coupler that splits the signals into clockwise and counter clockwise directions in the NALM configuration. The NALM loop is composed of an SOA (Inphenix C-Band IPSAD1505) and an integrated 45 cm-long SW. This waveguide is fabricated from a CMOS-compatible, highly doped silica glass52,53,78–83. As such, the SW features high mode confinement due to the small waveguide profile (2×2µm2), with group velocity dispersion coefficients of β2 ∼ 10 ps2km−1 and β3 ~ 0.26 ps3km−1 at 1550 nm, as well as a large third-order nonlinear coefficient of γ = 220 W−1km−1. The SW, together with the phase shift mechanism between the two counter-propagating fields, performs the overall nonlinear activation function of the reservoir52,53. The SOA operates between the linear and nonlinear regimes, far from saturation, to avoid instabilities. These include self-oscillation and chaotic behaviors, as well as noise amplification and signal fluctuations, which would be detrimental to the current tasks. A polarization controller (PC) was used to select and optimize the transmission power of one field component, specifically either the transverse electromagnetic or magnetic field. Simultaneously, an optical bandpass filter (200 GHz) was used to limit the spectral bandwidth of the propagation fields, thereby improving the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and system stability by eliminating unwanted amplified spectral components. A 90:10 optical coupler is used to extract a fraction of the optical power from the loop to obtain a readout of the dynamic evolution of the node states, utilizing high-bandwidth photodiodes (PDs, Finisar XPDV21x0R series, 50 GHz bandwidth) and a digital oscilloscope (OS, Agilent DSO-x92804a, 28 GHz bandwidth). An additional OS is employed to perform the nonlinear recovery task. The overall length of the cavity is 14 m, corresponding to a round-trip time of approximately τr = 75 ns.

Information encoding and readout
We encode information (i.e., bits) into time-dependent vectors ui(n) by means of different arbitrary waveform generators (AWGs) (Keysight M8196A, 92 GSa s−1, 2 channels each), each driving an equal number of electro-optical Mach-Zehnder intensity modulators (IMs) (Optilab IML-1550-40-PM-V-HER, 40 GHz, polarization-maintaining, high extinction ratio, Vπ = 3 V). All modulators were synchronized using an external clock. The IMs were excited by the time-varying voltage signal containing the data, which in turn modulated the independent laser modes (i.e., the wavelength channels) produced by a narrowband continuous multi-wavelength (CW) source (ID Photonics CoBrite DXG, 4 outputs, linewidth <100 kHz). An additional CW source (Tunics T100S-HP, single output, linewidth <5 MHz) was employed to provide the fifth channel. The injected power per channel ranged from 1 mW to 5 mW, depending on the task. The applied voltage to the IMs varied between [-Vπ/2, Vπ/2], ensuring operation within their linear regime. When multi-processing is performed, the input channels are injected into the device via wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) using a waveshaper (WS).

The reservoir nodes are established by first sampling and holding the input signal containing data for a duration τ ≈ τr, then multiplying the signal by a uniformly distributed, multi-level random mask R(n), with values ranging between −1 and 1. The mask has a sampling period τ and duration θ per level, such that Ein(n) = u(n) * R(n), where Ein(n) is the resulting input signal to the device. This procedure maps the signal onto a higher-dimensional space by generating a number of ‘virtual’ node states (i.e., internal variables)84, the number of which is given by Nv = τ/θ. A slight desynchronization, δ ≈ θ, was applied to the sampling period τ on the AWG input sequence to ensure that all node states were dependent on neighboring nodes17.

For dense encoding, we input more than one bit of information (nb) in the reservoir per round-trip τr. We apply the sample and hold procedure over the asynchronous sampling rate (i.e., the inverse of the masking rate) of duration τ0 = τr/nb + δ0 to generate N' time-multiplexed transient states of duration θ0 = τ0/N0, for each τ0 time interval.

The small desynchronization δ0 ≈ θ0 between the sampling and injection rates causes a progressive shift in the input seen by adjacent virtual nodes and by nodes across round-trips, ensuring that neighboring nodes access distinct input segments over time and maintain the data correlation required for reservoir computing processing.

The output states, x(n), are measured from the virtual nodes at duration θ (or θ0) by using the PDs and OS. De-multiplexing using the WS is applied in cases of parallel computations. The average output power ranges from 100 μW to 300 μW per individual input channel.

M-bit delayed XOR task
To formally describe the m-bit delayed XOR task85, we define the operation within a logical framework. Given the input bit sequence {xn} with delay n and the number of bits m, the output sequence {yn} can be described by the following equation:
yn = xn ⊕ xn−1 ⊕ xn−2 ⊕ ... ⊕ xn−m if n ≥ m
yn = xn if n < m
where xn and yn are the current and output bits at time n, respectively.

Time series prediction tasks
The Mackey-Glass (MG) time series is defined by the following equation:
ẏMG(t) = β yMG(t−τ) / (1 + yMGp(t−τ)) − h yMG(t)
in which yMG(t) is the output at a time t, τ is the delay time, β is the growth rate, h is the decay rate, and p is the nonlinear parameter. Parameters were set as follows: τ = 17, β = 0.2, h = 0.1, p = 10. To simulate MG time series behavior, t was discretized using a time step Δt = 1 to produce values x(t) at discrete time points t = qΔt for q = 0, 1, 2, . . . .

The 10th-order Nonlinear Auto Regressive Moving Average (NARMA10) series follows the equation
y(t+1) = 0.3y(t) + 0.05y(t) * Σ(i=0 to 9) y(t−i) + 1.5u(t)x(t−9) + 0.1
in which y(t) is the output at time t, while u(t) is the input, chosen as a random sequence from a uniform distribution U[0, 1]. Similarly to the MG task, we applied a discretized time step Δt = 1 to the NARMA10 time series temporal variable t.

The time series were simultaneously and independently encoded onto two wavelength channels generated by the multi-output CW source. Two IMs and AWG channels drove this process. Following the previously described single-bit encoding technique, both signals were multiplexed using the WS and then injected simultaneously into the device. They were then de-multiplexed and read with the OS. Offline training (as detailed in the following sections) was performed on the two datasets collected.

Nonlinear telecom signal recovery task
The nonlinearly distorted signal, which also carries information, was obtained by propagating the corresponding pristine signal through 60 km of SMF-28, with a dispersion parameter D = 18 ps nm−1 km−1 and an attenuation constant α = 0.24 dB km−1. An additional 1 m of highly nonlinear optical fiber (with γ = 0.78 W−1 km−1) was added to account for the full extent of nonlinear effects over longer propagation distances, which is typical in telecommunications networks. The distorted signal, carrying 5×(215 – 1) bits, was sequentially split into five subsequences of 215 – 1 bits each and then independently encoded into the five wavelength channels using five IMs and AWG channels. Each AWG channel was operated at ~6.5 GHz. All five channels were amplified to 5 mW using an erbium-doped fiber amplifier (EDFA, Keopsys, PEFA-SP-C-PM−27-B202), then multiplexed into the reservoir. The additional IM and AWG channel were used to create the temporal node transients θ0 time intervals by using the PDs and OS via time multiplexing. These were implemented at a masking rate of approximately 24 GHz, creating 4 virtual nodes with a 20-level random mask, thereby enabling the encoding of 488 bits per round-trip. Offline training was performed on datasets built from the output node states of all five de-multiplexed wavelength channels, using the training procedure described in the following section.

Offline training
We employed a k-fold cross-validation approach, with k set to 5 for the MG and NARMA10 tasks and to 10 for the nonlinear channel equalization task. We then split the output datasets, consisting of xi values, into equally sized k subsets. The machine learning (ML) model was trained using ridge regression on k−1 folds and validated on the remaining fold. This process was repeated k times, with each fold used once as the validation set. For each fold, we determined the model’s accuracy by calculating the normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) as
NRMSE = sqrt( < (yi − y0i)^2 > / σ^2 )
in which σ2 is the sample variance, y0i is the targeted output, and yi is the weighted output: yi = Σ(j=1 to Nv) Wout,ij xj.
Finally, we calculated the average error across all iterations to obtain a more robust estimate of the model’s overall performance.

Simulations for nonlinear channel equalization
We employed a 10,000-pseudorandom binary sequence (PRBS) extracted from the experimentally generated distorted signal. We then sampled the signal using ultra-dense encoding, mirroring the experimental procedure previously described. We injected 488 bits per cavity round-trip over four nodes into a single channel. The device response was numerically simulated using the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSE) and then implemented in MATLAB (see Supplementary Note 1).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript introduces a photonic neural network architecture built using 4×4 multimode interferometers (MMIs) and a
proposed multi-operand microring resonator (MMORR) for nonlinear operations. The primary goal is to provide a scalable
and energy-efficient solution for deep learning acceleration by addressing limitations of Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI)
and microring resonator (MRR) based networks. The authors present theoretical models, perform FDTD simulations, and
evaluate the architecture on standard image classification datasets (MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR-10). The work claims high
compute density and low power consumption. The proposal of MMIs combined with nonlinear MMORRs represents a
potentially promising approach to optical computing and deep learning acceleration. The authors attempt to incorporate
nonlinear optical activation functions directly into the architecture.
However there are multiple critical weaknesses. It is not clear how the operation of the MMORR-based nonlinear unit is
implemented and the simulations fail to illustrate the computing mechanism convincingly. How is the nonlinearity generated
in the MMORRs? Why is this approach is superior or even viable compared to known methods. The experimental
validations are insufficient. In particular the experimental results on CIFAR-10 show only a 54.5% accuracy—significantly
below state-of-the-art—and the authors do not explain this shortcoming or compare fairly with digital or hybrid solutions. The
compute density calculation ignores critical physical constraints like metal routing and electronic interface area, significantly
inflating the reported performance. No evidence is provided for multi-mode utilization, even though final metrics are derived
based on it.
The paper claims power efficiency but does not rigorously detail the power consumption of each optical or electrical
component, nor does it benchmark against known designs or standards.
The paper does not discuss practical issues such as variability, fabrication tolerance, and bandwidth associated with optical
nonlinearity.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In the manuscript “Scalable Photonic Reservoir for Parallel Machine Learning Applications”, the authors design a figure-
eight shaped nonlinear amplifying loop mirror architecture for photonic reservoir computing, claiming that a 20-TOPS-level of
computing power and a femto-joules-per-operation-level of efficiency are achieved. Even though the reported performances
and capability seem to be superior, several questions need to be clarified to make the statements convincing.
1. In figure 1, the authors proposed a double ring-resonator structure to implement an all-optical reservoir computing system.
While the physical architecture is clearly depicted, the manuscript lacks detail regarding how the weights associated with the
SOA and VOA are trained or simulated.
2. The manuscript presents several results on machine learning tasks. However, the specific neural network architectures
employed to achieve these results are not described in sufficient detail. What is the exact configuration of the network that is
deployed and mapped onto the proposed photonic hardware? Providing a clear and comprehensive description of the
network structure is essential for ensuring the clarity of the presented results.
3. The customized ring-resonating structure has a high risk for undesired self-exciting oscillations. How will you eliminate
such noises to make the computing stable and the results repeatable?
4. In Figure 4, the authors presented the original undistorted telecom signal and the distorted signal after propagation.
However, such a figure only visualizes a common nonideal propagation phenomenon, and has little relation with the
proposed research. The authors may need to provide the recovered signal shape after the proposed photonic reservoir
computing.
5. Figure 4 presents only a basic illustration of the time traces of the modulated field intensity before and after propagation.
However, the manuscript lacks a detailed analysis or interpretation of these results, which may leave readers confused
about the significance and implications of the figure. More detailed numerical analysis for the performance is necessary to
make the research more convincing.
6. The authors mentioned “scalable” in the title of the manuscript, however, there seems to be no discussions of computing
scalability in the results section. More extra details, comparisons, figures, curves, and / or discussions that related to the
network scale and system scalability is necessary to support the claims in the title.
7. In the system throughput analysis section, the manuscript does not clarify the clock frequency assumed in the numerical
calculations. Since throughput is inherently tied to the system’s operating frequency, the lack of this information hinders a
proper assessment of the reported performance.
8. In the energy efficiency analysis section, it remains unclear whether the authors have accounted for the energy
consumption and potential speed limitations introduced by peripheral components. These include, for example, the data
feeding mechanisms, data acquisition systems, and the voltage drivers required for modulating the weights. The authors are
encouraged to clarify whether these peripheral factors were considered in the analysis, and if not, to discuss their possible
influence on the practical implementation of the proposed system.
9. While the manuscript introduces a new NALM-based architecture, it lacks a comprehensive comparison with other
existing photonic computing approaches in terms of key performance metrics such as throughput, energy efficiency, and
computational accuracy. Including such comparisons would greatly strengthen the manuscript by highlighting the relative
advantages of the proposed design.
10. In addition, it would be beneficial if the authors could provide baseline performance metrics for the demonstrated
computing tasks using conventional methods (e.g., electronic computing method). Presenting such benchmarks would offer
valuable context for evaluating the practical benefits of the proposed photonic implementation.
In conclusion, the submitted manuscript reported a novel photonic reservoir computing architecture with claimed promising
performance and capability, but these mentioned questions need to be settled to further make the manuscript more
comprehensive and convincing.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This paper proposes and implements a wavelength-division-multiplexed (WDM) reservoir computing (RC) system that
enables parallel neuromorphic computation. As WDM-based RC has already been experimentally demonstrated in previous
studies (e.g., [1]), the main contribution of this paper lies in its implementation of a nonlinear delay system called the
nonlinear amplifying loop mirror (NALM). Although this system utilizes gain saturation in a semiconductor optical amplifier
(SOA), the principle itself has already been reported in prior works [2,3], and thus lacks sufficient novelty. While the
experimental demonstration is intriguing, the reported computational performance (20 tera operations per second) is lower
than that of previous studies ([1] 800 TOPS, [4] 200 TOPS), and therefore does not offer the level of impact typically
expected for a publication in Nature Communications. Accordingly, I do not recommend publication in Nature
Communications. I believe this work would be more suitably presented in journals such as Scientific Reports or
Communications Physics, once the following concerns are addressed.
Major comments:
- The introduction should briefly review prior works on WDM-based approaches (e.g., [1,4,5]) and clearly delineate the
differences between those studies and the present work. The authors should also cite earlier approaches that utilize SOA
gain saturation (e.g., [2,3,6]) and clarify how their approach differs from them. In particular, [3,6] introduce nonlinearity via
cross-gain saturation by injecting light into both ports of the SOA, and since the conceptual similarities are evident, the
distinctions must be made clear.
- The relationship between the mathematical model in the Supplementary Information, and the experimental parameters
(e.g., Gs and T_VOA shown in Fig. 2) is unclear. The correspondence between physical quantities such as Gs and T_VOA
and the parameters in equations (S1–S15) should be explicitly stated.
- Additionally, in Fig. 2, the units of T_VOA and Gs are given in volts (V), which are device-dependent parameters; as a
result, readers cannot determine what is actually being optimized. It would be preferable to express these quantities in terms

We sincerely thank the reviewer for taking the time to assess our Manuscript. However, we respectfully note that
several of the comments raised appear to pertain to a different topic or paper and do not reflect at all he content,
methodology, or scope of our work.
To clarify, our Manuscript focuses on a photonic reservoir computing architecture based on a nonlinear amplifying
loop mirror (NALM), with emphasis on dense temporal encoding, wavelength-multiplexed multi-task processing,
and experimental demonstrations across several machine learning benchmarks, including XOR tasks, time-series
predictions, and nonlinear channel recovery. In contrast, the reviewer’s comments appear to refer to the use of
multimode interferometers and multi-operand microring resonators, which are not employed in this Manuscript, for
image classification on datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, which are unrelated to the methodology and scope
of our work.

We thank the reviewer for considering our work and for recognizing the promising performance and potential of our
approach. To enhance the clarity and overall quality of the Manuscript, we have provided a detailed, point-by-point
response to all the concerns raised.
1. In figure 1, the authors proposed a double ring-resonator structure to implement an all-optical reservoir computing
system. While the physical architecture is clearly depicted, the manuscript lacks detail regarding how the weights
associated with the SOA and VOA are trained or simulated.
Response
Our approach is based on time-delay reservoir computing, as opposed to a spatial reservoir with trainable internal
weights. In this architecture, computation is distributed across virtual nodes, which are time-multiplexed samples of
a single nonlinear dynamical system governed by a delayed feedback loop.
Importantly, the internal reservoir weights are not trained. Instead, they are fixed and randomly defined through the
input masking procedure, as previously established (Appeltant et al., 2011). In our system, the random mask is
implemented via a sample-and-hold mechanism, and the values of the mask define the reservoir weights.
This was discussed in Section S1 of the Supplementary Information in the earlier submission on line 32 (now lines
32-33).
The virtual nodes represent transient states of the nonlinear system, sampled at equally spaced time intervals over
the delay period.
The only trainable weights in the reservoir are the readout weights, for which a linear regression is performed on the
collected node states to produce the output (see Methods). Indeed, the reservoir approach eliminates the need for
internal weight optimization, which is a core advantage of this paradigm.
To further clarify: our system does not train internal weights via the SOA or VOA. Rather, there are fundamental
factors that shape the reservoir’s dynamic response, which we have demonstrated through a detailed theoretical
analysis using our model. Using our model, we explicitly show how modifying these physical parameters affects
key reservoir properties, such as memory and nonlinear transformation capabilities, as was detailed in the
Supplementary Information (lines 115–120 in the earlier submission).
Moreover, we would like to point out that our device doesn’t implement a ring-resonator structure, but rather a
figure-8 shaped cavity, which is fundamentally different in terms of field propagation and nonlinear interaction.
ACTION TAKEN
 Besides having been mathematically derived on lines 114–129 of the Supplementary Information, we have also
revised lines 32–33 of the Supplementary Information and lines 103–107 of the Manuscript. In the latter, we
now state: 'Consistent with the RC paradigm, training was applied exclusively to the output weights, while the
internal node connection weights remained fixed. These internal weights are inherently defined by the device
configuration and the specific components employed, such as the SOA, the integrated SW, and the variable
optical attenuator (VOA) (see also Supplementary Information).’ This clarifies that only the output weights are
trained in the reservoir computing framework and further explains the roles of the SOA and VOA in the
reservoir dynamics.

architectures employed to achieve these results are not described in sufficient detail. What is the exact configuration
of the network that is deployed and mapped onto the proposed photonic hardware? Providing a clear and

It is indeed true that we didn’t sketch the corresponding network architecture. However, we consistently stated that
our NALM configuration implements a reservoir computer (e.g., lines 58-68 in the earlier Manuscript version, now

overall, tunable nonlinearity that our system can produce. Details on how the network configuration, i.e., the
reservoir, is established on the device setup were presented in the Methods section (see paragraph beginning on line

3. The customized ring-resonating structure poses a high risk of undesired self-excited oscillations. How will you
eliminate such noises to make the computing stable and the results repeatable?
Response
We thank the reviewer for bringing this important point to our attention. Self-excited oscillations are a known
dynamic in ring resonator-based structures; however, our architecture, based on a figure-eight configuration rather
than a resonant cavity, with an integrated spiral waveguide as the nonlinear element, inherently mitigates this issue.
This is in line with the findings in our previous work (Aadhi et al., 2019). We maintain the SOA bias below the
onset of nonlinear gain regimes, where Ikeda-type instabilities emerge. By operating safely within this threshold, the
system remains in a stable regime. As was detailed in the Methods section (lines 280-281 in the earlier Manuscript
version, now on lines 332-334), we operate the SOA below saturation, far from the region in which gain instabilities
and spontaneous oscillations typically emerge. Furthermore, our implementation of the NALM architecture includes

suppresses chaotic oscillatory behavior, such as square-wave and fast oscillations. In addition, this element limits
modulation instability gain, therefore, ensuring the stability of computing results.
Experimentally, we identify in Fig. 2(a–c) the specific regions of parameter space, defined by the SOA bias voltage
and VOA attenuation, where the device achieves high accuracy and low NRMSE. These regions are characterized

consistent performance across XOR, Mackey-Glass, NARMA10, and nonlinear channel recovery tasks further
reinforces the robustness of our architecture against noise-induced instabilities.

in our system.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This paper proposes and implements a wavelength-division-multiplexed (WDM) reservoir computing (RC) system
that enables parallel neuromorphic computation. As WDM-based RC has already been experimentally demonstrated
in previous studies (e.g., [1]), the main contribution of this paper lies in its implementation of a nonlinear delay
system called the nonlinear amplifying loop mirror (NALM).
We thank the reviewer for bringing this aspect to our attention. We were indeed aware of [1] work that had already
cited it in our Manuscript. However, we would like to take this opportunity to clarify further the key differences
between our work and references [1], [4], and [5], particularly regarding WDM-related aspects, which were also
raised in a later comment (Reviewer Comment #1).
A major distinction between our system and that of [1,4,5] lies in the scalability of the architecture, in terms of both
reservoir structure and detection overhead, which directly impacts processing capability, adaptability, and overall
hardware efficiency.
While these prior works differ in implementation, they share several common limitations:
1. The systems lack tunability, with the activation function, fading memory inherently constrained by the design,
limiting flexibility and adaptability to tackle different machine learning tasks.
2. The reservoir dynamics remain linear, with nonlinearity applied only at the input/output stages via electronics,
introducing Optical-to-Electrical-to-Optical (OEO) latency.
3. These systems do not support true task-level parallelism (or concurrency, defined in the Manuscript), as multiple
wavelength or spatial channels are typically used to decompose and distribute a single task across parallel streams,
rather than enabling independent execution of multiple distinct tasks.
In [1], the system employs spatio-temporal multiplexing, where each bit is delayed using fixed delay lines and
processed in separate reservoir units that act as masking nodes. This enables interleaved processing (i.e., not real
concurrency), hence adding throughput latency in input/readout. Moreover, operation is constrained to specific input
laser conditions (e.g., θ = T/N), and each reservoir unit requires a separate pulsed laser source, further limiting
flexibility and scalability. The system also requires 32 photodiodes per channel, resulting in significant detection
overhead.
In [4], a similar interleaving strategy replaces recurrent feedback with a linear structure where delayed bit streams
emulate memory. However, identical to [1], this fixes the node dimensionality and limits scalability. While
frequency channels can parallelize a task by mimicking the identical input (as we also demonstrate in Figure 3 in the
Manuscript), this system does not support task differentiation across channels. Importantly, the use of interleaving
for parallelization compromises true concurrency, as it introduces preprocessing latency that ultimately limits the
computational throughput, the actual processing speed of the device.
In [5], multiple wavelength channels are only used to increase reservoir complexity by mixing frequency-domain
nodes through a cascaded architecture. However, the system does not support independent reservoir tasks. Instead, it
increases the effective dimensionality of a single task through spectral coupling, without enabling per-channel
flexibility or parallel execution of tasks with varying complexity.
Across all three systems, nonlinearity is confined to the input and output layers and implemented electronically,
making the reservoir dynamics effectively linear. This reliance on electronic activation introduces OEO latency and
limits the exploitation of ultrafast, nonlinear effects intrinsic to the optical approach.
In contrast, besides computational scalability, our system is designed to allow a tunable control of the reservoir
properties. We use CW lasers with amplitude modulation to encode information, and reservoir properties are
reconfigurable via the configuration tunable parameters, such as the SAO and VAO driving voltages. This enables
us to process data with varying levels of complexity across multiple wavelength channels, all within a single shared
reservoir. Our architecture supports any signal speed, limited only by the upper limit of input/readout electronics
bandwidth, enabling a universal, fully reconfigurable optical computing platform. This flexibility is demonstrated
through our applications in XOR logic, time-series classification, and nonlinear channel equalization, all of which
utilize a unified reservoir.
Regarding the reviewer’s comment: ‘the main contribution of this paper lies in its implementation of a nonlinear
delay system called the nonlinear amplifying loop mirror (NALM).’
Our choice to employ a NALM configuration to realize our processing device is guided by its proven efficacy in
generating highly stable and controllable nonlinear interactions, essential for optical reservoir computing (Kues et
al., 2017; Aadhi et al., 2019; Xiong et al., 2023). Previous approaches, such as those based on unidirectional cavities
or cross-gain modulation, have limitations including fixed nonlinear dynamics and reduced task versatility (Duport
et al., 2012, 2016; Vandoorne et al., 2008).
In contrast, the NALM architecture inherently supports robust and controllable nonlinear response, relying
promising results demonstrated our previous studies (Aadhi et al. 2019, Optics Express, 27, 25251-25259), where
the figure-eight cavity configuration demonstrated high tunability and a very rich nonlinear dynamics response,
beneficial for advanced optical computing and reservoir computing tasks, in terms of fine classification of inputs.
Additionally, earlier studies, such as those by Adams et al. (1994) and Kues et al. (2017), underline the NALM’s
intrinsic advantages in stable nonlinear dynamics, making it particularly attractive for reliable optical reservoir
computing applications.
Besides the novel configuration we implemented, our work introduces several key architectural and operational
novelties not only in terms of speed. This may have been misinterpreted in the earlier Manuscript version due to a
lack of clarity. We want to summarize the novelty aspects of our work here as follows.
i. True concurrent multi-task processing, with each wavelength channel independently masked and processed in
parallel within the same reservoir units (stated on lines 83–90, demonstrated in the parallel execution of the MG
time-series and NARMA10 prediction tasks, along with the multi-channel recovery task).
ii. Computational throughput scalability is achieved by combining dense temporal encoding (each channel carries
multiple bits per round-trip, thereby enhancing information density and computational speed) with parallel
wavelength channels, allowing each channel to carry multiple bits per round-trip. This significantly enhances
information density and computational efficiency without requiring additional components or modifications to
the device architecture (see lines 208-212).
iii. Tunable nonlinearity embedded directly in the reservoir, enabled by the NALM mechanism and the presence of
an SOA operating in an unsaturated regime, allowing precise control over the nonlinear response and avoiding
the limitations associated with cross-gain saturation.
iv. High energy-efficiency compared to previous demonstrations, even those chip-based (see Table 1 in the
Manuscript).
Taken together, our work presents a qualitatively different approach to optical neuromorphic computing, focusing
on scalable, reconfigurable, and energy-efficient parallel processing, with experimentally demonstrated performance
from our device.
